thread.title: Dolby Laboratories: Still A Great Business And A Questionable Valuation - Dolby Laboratories, Inc. (NYSE:DLB)

author: Vince Martin
title: Dolby Laboratories: Still A Great Business And A Questionable Valuation - Dolby Laboratories, Inc. (NYSE:DLB)
text:
Dolby Laboratories ( DLB ) admittedly has outperformed my expectations. As growth stalled out in the beginning of the decade, the cash-heavy stock looked like a potential value trap. And I haven't quite come around to trusting the recent reversal to steady growth, most recently passing on the stock about a year ago.
DLB is up about 9% since then - a performance that looks better in the context of a barely 1% gain in the S&P 500 over the same period (and sub-3% appreciation for the Russell 3000). And the gains seemingly are well-deserved. FY18 (ending September) results look solid, with the company driving 8%+ revenue growth and an apparent expansion in adjusted margins. (Dolby's non-GAAP discussions are incomplete, but adding back adjustments to net income implies a ~12% rise in non-GAAP EBIT last year.) Three new initiatives - Dolby Voice, Dolby Vision, and Dolby Cinema - are growing quickly, and accounted for 8%+ of total revenue last year. And an explosion in the company's licensing revenue in the mobile category adds another - and larger - potential growth driver going forward.
But I still can't get behind the story here - in large part because valuation hardly looks all that attractive. Excluding share-based compensation - as Dolby itself does - from non-GAAP numbers leaves the stock looking reasonably priced, at ~19x earnings and 12.5x FY19 EBITDA (both figures back out cash and are calculated using the company's full-year FY19 guidance). But that comp is substantial: $71 million in fiscal 2018, over 6% of revenue. As I've pointed out before, even analysts - generally a tolerant bunch when it comes to non-GAAP adjustments - appear to add that sum back to their own EPS estimates.
Including that spend, DLB's enterprise multiples move closer to 15x EBITDA and 23x earnings. With a couple of concerns appearing in Q4, that still looks like too much. But, again, I've said that before.
Where Dolby Stands Now As noted, FY18 was a strong year, with solid growth across the board and modest margin expansion. The most noteworthy performance came in the company's Mobile category, which includes smartphones and tablets. Dolby doesn't break out direct revenue, but figures from the 10-K show the category went from 13% of revenue in FY17 to 20% in FY18.
That suggests a 68% increase in category sales last year. A huge recovery (essentially a back payment) boosted Q1 revenue, and drove a chunk of that growth. Mobile revenue rose about $40 million, based on figures from the 10-Q , and the single recovery drove a significant amount of that growth. Still, the year-over-year increase in dollars was in the range of $85 million, suggesting likely at least 40% growth for the full year even beyond the Q1 recovery.
The strength there is quite a surprise, given revenue appears to have been flat to down in FY15 and FY16 before a ~13% increase in FY17. Adding Apple ( AAPL ) as a customer no doubt helped. But the company highlighted multiple wins over the course of the year, including China's Huawei, while Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ) added the newer Dolby Atmos (and the AC-4 codec) for the Galaxy S9 and other phones.
Management has insisted on recent quarters that there's still more room for growth ahead, with CEO Kevin Yeaman calling mobile "a big opportunity" on the Q3 call . Despite the comparison against the Q1 FY18 recovery, the company guided for growth on the Q4 call in FY19 as well.
There is a tailwind there from recast FY18 numbers under ASC 606 - which are expected to have about a $72 million impact, the "majority" of which is coming from mobile (that forecast for y/y growth is coming on a recast basis, which is expected to have minimal impact on FY19 numbers). And the recast itself does suggest that FY18 numbers, as originally reported, had some help from sales that would have been booked in earlier years under the new accounting guidelines. (Dolby is not revising revenue from past years, per the call.) Still, there's clearly a step-up in growth here - with Dolby benefiting despite (and possibly because of) what appears to be a stagnant market on a unit basis.
Elsewhere, there really isn't much in the way of surprises. PC revenue continues to fall, in part due to fewer units being shipped with optical disks. Consumer electronics sales have been solid, with increasing soundbar adoption. The broadcast business (set-top boxes and TVs) has been flattish the last two years, though a new STB cycle could provide a catalyst going forward. Other revenue (gaming, automotive, Dolby Cinema, and Dolby Voice) looks somewhat disappointing, with a point loss of total share suggesting low- to mid-single-digit growth. Lower recoveries in automotive were a factor, per the 10-K. Product revenue growth has stalled out, but guidance for FY19 suggests a strong increase, with products and services (the latter 2% of revenue) guided up ~30-50%, thanks to sales of Dolby Cinema products and videoconferencing equipment under Dolby Voice.
The trends seen of late, then, remained largely intact in FY18:
Source: author from DLB filings; revenue calculated by multiplying percentage figures from 10-K by total licensing revenue, and so rounding errors possible
Initial FY19 guidance on the Q4 call suggests a continuation of recent trends, with projected growth in broadcast and the big jump in products the two biggest potential trajectory changes. PCs are guided flat to down, Consumer Electronics should continue to grow, and Mobile revenue, as noted, is expected to increase off the recast numbers. The midpoint of revenue guidance suggests 7.5% growth off the initially reported FY18 base, with adjusted EBIT margins down narrowly (my numbers have the midpoint of guidance projecting a 6% y/y in adjusted operating income). Given that Dolby nicely beat initial guidance for FY18, some investors might price in even better growth.
Where Dolby Goes From Here There's certainly a path here where DLB continues to grind higher. Looking at the breakdown of FY18 revenue, there now looks to be a decent amount of exposure to potentially growing areas:
Category FY18 Revenue % of Total FY18 Growth FY19 Growth Broadcast $412M 35% -1% positive Mobile $211M 18% +68% positive on recast basis Other $159M 14% +3% positive Consumer Electronics $148M 13% +18% positive PC $127M 11% -12% flat to down Products $95M 8% -1% up 30%+ Services $20M 2% -3% likely up Numbers not recast. Licensing revenue figures are author calculations derived from 10-K figures; products and services are disclosed separately. FY19 guidance from Q4 call. Numbers do not foot due to rounding.
That said, there's a clear reliance on two key categories where underlying growth in the end market is rather weak - meaning Dolby needs to grow through adoption - not market volume. That's certainly possible, if not probable. Dolby has shown huge success in TVs of late, continually racking up new partners. LG now is shipping units with both Atmos and Dolby Vision - potentially setting the trend for other high-end manufacturers and further boosting revenue in broadcast beyond 2019. Orange ( ORAN ) is doing the same with set-top boxes, per the Q4 call, and that upgrade cycle could offset secular weakness in those products.
In mobile, both Atmos and Vision are seeing wider adoption - a trend that similarly could continue as manufacturers try and differentiate their products and keep ASP increases intact.
That ability - to grow revenue in stagnant end markets - really is key to the DLB case at the moment, given how much revenue is coming from those areas (close to two-thirds if an investor adds in PCs). Because if Dolby can grow there, that amplifies growth that should come from the three new initiatives: Voice, Vision, and Cinema.
And there's one number, that depending on the eye of the beholder, either supports or undercuts the argument for those initiatives: the fact that FY18 revenue from Voice, Vision, and Dolby Cinema was $100 million.
The reason for optimism toward the new initiatives could be precisely that the figure still is rather small, at ~8% of FY18 revenue. Yeaman said in the Q&A of the Q4 call that he expected a similar growth rate from those businesses in FY19 as the ~67% ($60M to $100M) seen in fiscal 2018. That in turn gets the group to a more significant ~13% of FY19 sales - and makes it a more powerful growth driver going forward.
But the figure also might suggest real room for multi-year expansion. After all, efforts with those three technologies are still at the beginning. For Dolby Cinema, AMC Entertainment ( AMC ) remains the biggest partner - and has talked optimistically about pricing (a ~70% premium, per AMC conference calls) and future growth. The company closed FY18 with 170 locations - and an additional 220-plus "open or committed" around the world, per the K. Growth in China, in particular, seems a major potential driver: Dolby already has seven partners in that country.
In Voice, Dolby Voice Room for "huddle rooms" was only launched last year. Partnerships with BlueJeans and HighFive are in the early stages. Vision added PCs in Q1 (with Lenovo ( OTCPK:LNVGY )) and the Microsoft ( MSFT ) Xbox One in Q3. The dual Atmos-Vision offering, in particular, seems a potential winner, as the company builds an 'ecosystem' around Voice that extends from creators to manufacturers to distributors. (Netflix ( NFLX ) uses both products already, as do multiple OTT players worldwide.)
Even assuming some deceleration in revenue from the three initiatives going forward, due to both a higher base and lapping recent wins, these growth areas should add a couple points of annual revenue growth for years to come. Given high-80s gross margins, that alone seems to support sustained profit growth for several years, and perhaps enough on its own to in turn keep multiples at a reasonably high level.
There's a bear case to make here, too, however - and that case actually strengthened with the Q4 release. For one, growth outside of those three initiatives looks pretty slim, at 4.6% in FY18 (with pretty much all of that from mobile, most likely) and under 3% in FY16 and FY17.
Secondly, the group disappointed in FY18. As recently as the Q3 call, Yeaman was projecting that sales from the three new initiatives would double year-over-year - to about $120 million. The actual figure came in at just over $100 million. Management attributed the miss to timing issues with Dolby Cinema - as new locations from Chinese partners were pushed out into Q1.
The problem, though, is that the timing shift isn't the only reason. Q3 projections for the initiatives - again, a big part of the bull case here - were 30 points off . That's a huge number. But it's also a number that suggests that it's Dolby Cinema - not Vision - that is driving the overall figure. (Voice clearly is a much smaller portion, per commentary.) That suggestion is supported by both the magnitude of the guidance miss and the projections for $30-50 million-plus in products and services revenue growth next year - much of which is coming from Dolby Cinema products (in addition to existing licensing agreements for the theaters themselves).
If Dolby Cinema is driving the growth, then how big are Vision sales? It would appear the figure is relatively small - something like $80 million at most next year, or 6%+ of total revenue. (That seems likely aggressive given expected growth from Voice in FY19.) And is Dolby Cinema a business that should be valued even in line with the rest of Dolby? IMAX ( IMAX ) is the obvious peer - and that stock is trading at under 18x CY18 consensus EPS, backing out a modest amount of net cash, and threatening a six-year low.
There's also the issue that a key growth area is China - and given potential economic turmoil in that country, it seems unwise to dismiss the possibility that slower-than-expected Q4 growth is a single-quarter problem. More broadly, Dolby Cinema margins are going to be smaller (owing to the proportion of product sales) and the growth profile could be seen as less attractive than even stagnant end markets like smartphones and TVs.
If Dolby Cinema is the biggest of the three initiatives right now, as appears to be the case, that seems to lessen the attractiveness of that total growth opportunity. And the Q4 miss adds some near-term risks and concerns as well.
Valuation All told, from here, DLB at $68 looks like a bet on management. If Dolby is right, and mobile growth will be strong for years, broadcast sales will re-accelerate, and the three initiatives will increase revenue 60%+ in FY19, DLB likely gains over the next twelve months, and potentially beyond. There is some room for multiple expansion here given the attractiveness of the licensing model, and tack that on to underlying FY19 growth and DLB can rise 15-20%, easily (think 10% EBITDA growth, at the high end of guidance, and 1-2 turns in multiple expansion).
A mixed year for the business seemingly leads to a mixed year for the stock. If new initiatives, in particular, come in below the heady growth modeled, multiple expansion here gets a bit tougher. Dolby looks more like a business grinding out upside, and it's tough to see how multiples expand in that outcome. In fact, they likely contract, if modestly so.
And there's still a bearish scenario here, even if shorts have moved on from a stock that occasionally was a target. If Q4 concerns from Dolby Cinema persist, and mobile in particular disappoints, the mid-term growth profile here changes markedly - and not for the better. I still think there's a reasonable bear case scenario where DLB drops back to ~15x EPS (backing out stock comp), which suggests a tumble toward $50.
The cash-heavy balance sheet and the licensing model obviously limit both risk and reward - but from here, the two look balanced at best. DLB needs to win in its new initiatives, and it needs growth in stagnant end markets. That seems like a lot to ask - and it certainly seems like if Dolby falls short on either front, what remains a reasonably expensive stock could get cheaper.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
